title: Hegseth's Feud with Lawmakers Threatens Trump's $1.5 Trillion Defense Plan
snippet: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's combative posture toward Capitol Hill has fractured long-standing bipartisan norms, jeopardizing President Trump's ambitious $1.5 trillion defense agenda amidst dwindling military stocks and looming midterm elections.
content:
WASHINGTON — For decades, national defense policy enjoyed a rare sanctuary from Washington's fierce partisan battles. Today, that bipartisan consensus is collapsing, largely fueled by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's increasingly hostile relationship with lawmakers on Capitol Hill.

The rift has severely endangered President Donald Trump’s record $1.5 trillion defense budget request. With just weeks left in the legislative calendar and military hardware depleted after months of conflict with Iran, lawmakers from both parties warn that the Pentagon's ambitious national security agenda is running out of time.

The strain was laid bare earlier this year during a private exchange, when Hegseth asked a senior Republican lawmaker to estimate the odds of Congress passing the administration's massive budget. The lawmaker's response was sharp: the chances were about the same as Hegseth winning Senate confirmation a second time.

A Fractured Bipartisan Consensus

The annual National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) has successfully passed Congress for 65 consecutive years, serving as a reliable benchmark for military spending and troop policy. However, this year's legislative push has completely stalled in the Senate after barely surviving a House vote that saw more Republicans oppose it than Democrats support it.

The core of the dispute centers on the administration's unprecedented $1.5 trillion funding package. The proposal includes funding to replenish precision missiles and advanced drones, while directing billions toward high-profile presidential priorities, such as a national 'Golden Dome' missile defense system and official efforts to rename the Defense Department as the 'War Department.'

To navigate resistance, the Trump administration divided the budget request into two tracks: a $1.15 trillion primary spending package requiring bipartisan backing, and a separate $350 billion measure intended to pass via party-line votes. Yet, Republicans have been unable to unite around a strategy to pass even the single-party share.

"The people who have been around for a few days have seen what normal looks like," said Rep. Joe Courtney (D-CT). "We’re not living in normal."

Rising Hostility and Excluded Lawmakers

Lawmakers point to Hegseth's aggressive tactics as a primary driver of the gridlock. During congressional appearances, Hegseth has repeatedly lashed out at critics, previously labeling Democratic and Republican dissenters as "reckless, feckless and defeatist."

Additionally, the Pentagon broke long-standing national security protocol by barring Democrats from several classified briefings regarding the $350 billion budget portion. Trump administration officials justified the move over concerns regarding press leaks, but the exclusion alienated even GOP allies.

"It's as shockingly unprofessional as anything I see," said Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), describing Hegseth's combative posture toward lawmakers.

Senior Republicans have expressed similar frustrations. Rep. Austin Scott (R-GA) bluntly noted that securing major funding requires coalition-building: "The way Hegseth treats people is a problem."

In defense of the administration, Pentagon spokesman Joel Valdez stated that Hegseth remains open to good-faith dialogue. "Lawmakers understand exactly how critical the National Defense Authorization Act and defense appropriations are to military readiness," Valdez said. "We do not expect them to deliberately cripple the force or our warfighting capability simply to score political points."

Operational Risks Mount as Midterms Approach

The political stalemate arrives at a perilous moment for the U.S. military. U.S. Central Command estimates that military operations involving Iran have already cost over $47 billion, forcing the Pentagon to divert funds from routine maintenance and training programs.

GOP members warn that adversaries are paying close attention to the dysfunction in Washington. "Russia and China are questioning whether or not we have the resources and the ability to quickly replace dwindling stocks and ammunition," warned Sen. Mike Rounds (R-SD).

With the upcoming midterm elections likely to shift control of the House to Democrats, Hegseth faces mounting pressures. Beyond budget gridlock, the Defense Secretary faces potential impeachment motions from conservative figures over the conduct of the Iran war, alongside bipartisan opposition to several of his key leadership appointments.

As Gen. Dan Caine, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, conducts quiet diplomacy breakfasts with lawmakers to smooth over tensions, many on Capitol Hill remain skeptical that the relationship can be salvaged in time to pass the historic budget.
